question: What is the main goal of disease prevention in public health?

options.A: Finding new surgical methods for complex chronic illnesses
options.B: Stopping health problems before they start or halting their progress
options.C: Reducing the cost of pharmaceutical manufacturing plants
options.D: Increasing hospital admission rates for routine checkups

explanation: You've got this! Prevention is all about stopping illness proactively before it takes hold, rather than just treating symptoms later.

question: Why should nurses care about population-focused public health prevention?

options.A: It allows nurses to stop working directly with individual sick patients
options.B: It replaces the need for basic clinical bedside nursing skills entirely
options.C: It helps nurses address environmental and social factors affecting entire communities
options.D: It guarantees that hospitals will never experience overcrowding issues

explanation: Great thinking! Looking at populations helps us see the bigger picture—treating the whole community, not just one patient in a hospital bed.

question: Which activity is a classic example of primary prevention?

options.C: Performing a blood pressure screening clinic
options.D: Providing physical therapy after a stroke

explanation: Vaccines protect healthy people from contracting a specific disease in the first place, which defines primary prevention. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h2)

question: How is primordial prevention different from primary prevention?

options.A: Primordial prevention relies entirely on medications, while primary relies on surgery
options.B: Primordial prevention is only used for infectious diseases, while primary is for chronic illnesses
options.C: Primordial prevention targets broad social and environmental policies, while primary targets specific health habits
options.D: Primordial prevention happens after a disease is diagnosed, while primary happens before

explanation: Think of primordial prevention as tackling big-picture societal conditions, while primary prevention focuses on personal habits and exposures like vaccines.

question: What is the main purpose of secondary prevention?

options.A: Rehabilitation after a permanent disability occurs
options.B: Preventing a healthy person from ever getting sick
options.C: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment of a disease
options.D: Creating broad national economic health policies

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about catching issues early through screening before severe symptoms take over. Spot it early, treat it early!

question: A nurse is teaching range-of-motion exercises to a patient recovering from a stroke. Which level of prevention is this?
explanation: Rehabilitation and preventing further disability from an established disease fall under tertiary prevention. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h3)

question: What is the main goal of a health screening test?

options.A: To provide a definitive and final medical diagnosis
options.B: To replace the need for primary prevention vaccines
options.C: To cure a chronic illness without needing further treatment
options.D: To identify unrecognized disease in apparently healthy people

explanation: Screenings help us catch hidden health issues early in people who feel completely fine, giving them a head start on care.

question: What should happen immediately after a patient's blood pressure check flags a high reading at a community health fair?

options.A: Immediate prescription of lifelong high blood pressure medication
options.B: Reassurance that screening tests are always fully accurate
options.C: Referral for formal diagnostic evaluation by a primary provider
options.D: Immediate admission to an intensive care hospital unit

explanation: Remember, a screening just raises a warning flag—it doesn't give a final diagnosis. The patient needs proper medical follow-up to confirm!

question: How does active immunization protect the body against future infections?

options.A: By destroying all existing white blood cells in the bloodstream
options.B: By transferring ready-made antibodies directly from another person
options.C: By stimulating the immune system to produce its own antibodies
options.D: By providing instant chemical disinfection on the skin surface

explanation: Active immunity acts like a gym workout for your immune system, teaching it to build its own antibodies and remember germs for later.

question: Which scenario is an example of acquiring passive immunity?

options.A: An adolescent developing long-term immunity after a live vaccine
options.B: A healthy adult receiving a routine tetanus booster shot
options.C: An infant receiving protective antibodies through breast milk
options.D: A child recovering completely from a natural chickenpox infection

explanation: Passive immunity involves receiving ready-made antibodies from an external source rather than making them yourself. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h5)

question: What is a key requirement for successful community health education?

options.A: Using complex medical terminology to ensure scientific accuracy
options.B: Adapting the teaching to the cultural context and literacy levels of the audience
options.C: Relying exclusively on written pamphlets without verbal explanations
options.D: Conducting all teaching sessions inside high-tech hospital seminar rooms

explanation: Teaching only works when your audience truly understands it. Always speak in a way that connects with their daily lives and culture!

question: A community health nurse notices an increase in diarrhea cases during the rainy season. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Educating local families on safe water storage and oral rehydration
options.B: Ordering advanced genetic testing for all community members
options.C: Recommending immediate surgical procedures for every household
options.D: Waiting for patients to arrive at the central hospital for intravenous therapy

explanation: Simple community education on clean water and oral rehydration saves lives quickly and stops outbreaks right at the source.

question: Which of these is a core responsibility of a nurse in primary health care?

options.A: Setting national monetary policies for healthcare budgets
options.B: Conducting major surgical operations in tertiary hospitals
options.C: Assessing community needs and providing direct health education
options.D: Manufacturing pharmaceutical drugs in a laboratory setting

explanation: As a nurse, checking what your community lacks and teaching them how to stay healthy is a huge part of your primary care role.

question: Why is building trust with community leaders so important for a public health nurse?

options.A: It helps ensure that community members accept and participate in prevention programs
options.B: It eliminates the need to collect health data from individual families
options.C: It guarantees that the nurse will receive financial bonuses from the government
options.D: It allows the nurse to bypass standard medical regulations and protocols

explanation: People listen to leaders they trust. When community leaders back your health programs, the local residents will be much more eager to join in!
